scope.start: 8b: a woman who tells the man to give the loaf to a poor person (continuing the cases of redirected gifts)
scope.end: 9b: the kal va'chomer and the hekesh that would let a Hebrew maidservant be acquired through intercourse, and the verse that excludes her

sections.title: Rejecting While Seeming to Accept: Charity, Doubled Words, a Single Word
sections.gist: Continuing the cases of a woman who answers a proposal by redirecting or demanding the gift, three replies that fail to accept *kiddushin*: sending the bread to a poor person, a doubled “give, give,” and, in dispute, a single “give.”

children.title: “Give It to a Poor Person”: Her Duty of Charity Is His Too
children.gist: Telling him to give the loaf to a poor person is no acceptance, even when the poor person depends on her.

bullets.text: The man says, “Be betrothed to me with this loaf.” She answers, “Give it to a poor person.” She is not betrothed, even if the poor person regularly depends on her for food.
The reason: she can say, “Just as I am obligated to support him, so are you.” Sending the bread there shows no agreement to the betrothal.
Giving *tzedakah* to someone who regularly relies on you has a special priority, close to an obligation. Even that bond does not turn her redirecting of the bread into acceptance.

children.title: “Give, Give,” “Give to Drink,” “Throw, Throw”: Doubled Replies Mean Nothing
children.gist: Three stories in which a woman asks for something, the man makes it conditional on betrothal, and her doubled reply is ruled no acceptance at all.

bullets.text: A man was selling strings of glass beads. A woman asked for one string. He: “If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?” She: “Give, give.” Rav Chama: “give, give” is nothing.
A man was drinking wine in a store. A woman asked for a cup. He made the same condition. She: “Give to drink, give it to me to drink.” Rav Chama: this too is nothing.
A man was picking dates from a palm. A woman asked him to throw her two. He made the same condition. She: “Throw, throw.” Rav Zevid: this is nothing.
The doubled demand is impatience to get the item. She brushes his condition aside rather than agreeing to it; in the Gemara's words she was mocking him.
Why two dates rather than one? Perhaps a single date might not be worth a *perutah*.

children.title: A Single “Give”: Ravina vs. Rav Sama bar Rakta
children.gist: If she answered with one word only, Ravina says she is betrothed and Rav Sama bar Rakta swears she is not; the halakha follows him.

bullets.text: Question: what if she said only “give,” “give to drink,” or “throw,” without the doubling?
Ravina: she is betrothed. Rav Sama bar Rakta, with an oath, “By the king's crown!”: she is not betrothed.
The halakha: she is not betrothed.
Rabbeinu Chananel (cited by the Rashba) reads the oath as: even had he given her the king's crown, she would not be betrothed, since the way she answered shows she never agreed to marry him.

sections.title: Three Rulings: Silk Needs No Appraisal, R. Elazar, and Collateral
sections.gist: The Gemara settles earlier disputes (silk needs no appraisal, a partial payment betroths, collateral does not), and the shiur adds Tosafot on precious stones.

bullets.text: Silk garments worth more than a *perutah* need no appraisal before a woman is betrothed with them.
This follows Rabba against Rav Yosef, who required the silk to be appraised.
The halakha follows R. Elazar: if he promised her 100 dinars and gave her one, she is betrothed.
The halakha follows Rava in the name of Rav Nachman: if he promised 100 dinars and gave only collateral, it is not a valid betrothal.

Tosafot (the Ri, with Rabbeinu Tam): silk's value is familiar, so people rarely misjudge it. Precious stones can be wildly misjudged, and she may have accepted on a mistaken value, so they may need appraisal. The worry is her understanding, not whether the stone is worth a *perutah*.
This Tosafot lies behind the custom of a plain band under the *chuppah*. An object of clear value, worth a *perutah*, given before witnesses, poses no inherent problem.

sections.title: Shtar Kiddushin: Its Form, Who Writes It, Whether It Follows the Get
sections.gist: Betrothal by document: the baraita's form, R. Zeira bar Memel's question why the husband writes, the minor and the *bogeret*, and whether the document must be written for her and with her consent.

children.title: The Baraita: Paper or Earthenware, Worth Less Than a Perutah
children.gist: The husband writes to the father, “Your daughter is betrothed to me,” on any material, and it betroths by its content, not its value.

bullets.text: The husband writes to the young woman's father, on paper or earthenware: “Your daughter is betrothed (*mekudeshet*) to me,” or “betrothed (*me'oreset*) to me,” or “Your daughter is to me as a wife.” She is betrothed.
The material need not be worth a *perutah*, since she is not betrothed through its value.
The *shtar kiddushin* works through its words, not as money. It was probably rarely used in practice, which is why its laws are thinly developed.

Rashba: it needs names and a date, like any document. Ritva and others: “You are betrothed to me” written on anything suffices. Whether he must also say the words aloud when handing it over is debated.

children.title: Who Writes the Document: The Seller in a Sale, the Husband Here
children.gist: R. Zeira bar Memel asks why the husband, who is like a buyer, writes. Rava answers from each verse, the verses turn out to cut both ways, and Rava concludes that both rules are a received tradition.

children.title: R. Zeira bar Memel's Challenge; Rava: Each Follows Its Own Verse
children.gist: In a sale the seller writes “my field is sold to you,” but here the husband writes; Rava answers that each rule follows the verse that frames it.

bullets.text: R. Zeira bar Memel objects: this is unlike a bill of sale. There the seller writes to the buyer, “My field is sold to you.” Here the husband, who is like the buyer, writes, “Your daughter is betrothed to me.”
The woman or her father is the one transferring, like a seller, yet they do not write the document.
Rava: each follows its verse. “And sells of his ancestral land” (Vayikra 25:25) makes the sale depend on the seller. “If a man takes a woman” (Devarim 22:13) makes betrothal depend on the husband.

children.title: “Yiknu” or “Yikkanu,” “Yikach” or “Yakiach”: The Verses Cut Both Ways
children.gist: A verse in Yirmiyahu points to the buyer; rereading it to fit the Torah invites rereading “takes” as “is given,” so the verse-based answer fails.

bullets.text: Objection: Yirmiyahu 32:44, “Men shall buy (*yiknu*) fields for money,” points to the buyer.
Answer: read it *yikkanu*, “shall be sold,” to match the Torah's “and sells.”
Then by the same logic read “*ki yikach*” as “*ki yakiach*,” “when he is given,” to match “I gave my daughter to this man” (Devarim 22:16). The verses no longer settle who writes.

children.title: A Received Tradition, or “I Took the Deed of Purchase”
children.gist: Rava calls both rules a tradition merely attached to verses; alternatively, the seller's writing is shown by Yirmiyahu's taking the deed.

bullets.text: Rava: the verses do not prove it. These are a received tradition (*hilkheta*), and the Sages attached them to verses.
Alternatively, for the sale: Yirmiyahu says, as buyer, “And I took the deed of purchase” (32:11), showing that the seller writes it.

Tosafot: the sale needs no tradition, since it follows from the verses; only the husband's writing of the *shtar kiddushin* is tradition. On the Rambam's view, *halakha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* means rules that could never be derived from the text.
Many rishonim treat any derivation from the Prophets as an *asmakhta*. Yirmiyahu's purchase in Anatot, on the eve of exile, was a prophetic sign of return.

children.title: Minor or Bogeret: Whose Wording, Whose Consent
children.gist: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman: for a minor the document addresses the father and needs his consent; for a *bogeret* it addresses her and needs hers.

bullets.text: Written to the father (“Your daughter is betrothed to me,” etc.), whether given to her father or to her, she is betrothed with her father's consent, provided she is not yet a *bogeret*.
For a minor the father is the principal party in the betrothal, not merely her agent.

Written to her (“You are hereby betrothed to me,” “You are hereby to me as a wife”), whether given to her father or to her, she is betrothed with her consent, provided she is a *bogeret*, under her own authority.
The rishonim: a father has no authority over a *bogeret*, so handing it to him works only if she appointed him her agent to receive it.

children.title: Does the Shtar Follow the Get? Lishmah and Her Consent
children.gist: Reish Lakish derives from *havayah le'yetziah* that the document must be written *lishmah*; *amora'im* split on whether it also needs her consent; and a mishnah requiring both parties' consent is read as dealing with dowry agreements.

children.title: Shelo Lishmah: Compare to the Get, or to Betrothal Money?
children.gist: Reish Lakish asks whether a betrothal document written not for her is valid, and resolves from “and she departs… and becomes” that it must be *lishmah*, like a *get*.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish asks about a *shtar kiddushin* written *shelo lishmah*, not for this particular woman.
If becoming betrothed is juxtaposed with leaving a marriage (*havayah le'yetziah*): as a *get* must be *lishmah*, so must the betrothal document.
If the modes of betrothal are juxtaposed with each other: betrothal money need not be coins minted for her, so neither need the document be written for her.
Reish Lakish resolves it: betrothal is juxtaposed with divorce, “And she departs out of his house, and goes and becomes” (Devarim 24:2). The document must be *lishmah*.
Picture a scribe filling a stack of forms reading “You are betrothed to me,” with the name left blank, to sell to all comers: that is a document written *shelo lishmah*.

Reish Lakish champions this comparison throughout the tractate, while R. Yochanan limits it (the clash on 44a, where Reish Lakish cries “*havayah le'yetziah*” three times). A divorcée is not simply a woman returned to her former status, so how far the two processes mirror each other matters.
The Rif cites the Yerushalmi: only a document worth less than a *perutah* depends on the rules of a *get*. One worth a *perutah* betroths as money anyway, so the practical question is narrow.

children.title: Written for Her but Without Her Knowledge: Two Readings of One Hekesh
children.gist: Rava and Ravina say she is betrothed, Rav Pappa and Rav Sherevya say not; Rav Pappa derives both views from the same comparison to the *get*.

bullets.text: A document written *lishmah* but without her knowledge: Rava and Ravina say she is betrothed. Rav Pappa and Rav Sherevya say she is not.
Rav Pappa states their reason: a *get* must be *lishmah* but may be written without her consent, so the betrothal document may be too.
His own reason: a *get* requires the consent of the one transferring, the husband. In betrothal the one transferring is the woman, so her consent is required.
This consent argument does not arise for betrothal money, which has little structural tie to divorce.

chart.caption: A betrothal document written for her but without her knowledge
rows: Written *lishmah*; her consent is not needed
Written for her suffices, even without her knowledge
The consent of the one transferring (the husband) is needed
The one transferring is the woman, so her consent is needed

children.title: Objection from a Mishnah: Documents of Stipulation, Not of Betrothal
children.gist: A mishnah requires both parties' consent for “documents of betrothal,” but it means dowry agreements, the pledges that Rav Giddel says are acquired by speech.

bullets.text: Objection from a mishnah (Bava Batra 167b): documents of betrothal and marriage are written only with the consent of both. Does this not mean actual betrothal documents, requiring her consent?
No: it means documents of stipulation (*shtarei pesikta*), which set out the dowry. These are money contracts and need both sides' consent.
As Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav: the fathers agree how much each will give; if the couple then become betrothed, the pledges are acquired. These are matters acquired through speech alone.
Rashi: the terms and sums each side commits to, like today's *tena'im*. In Talmudic times *kiddushin* often came months before the wedding, yet breaking it required a *get*.

sections.title: Kiddushin by Bi'ah: Its Source, the Betrothed Virgin, the Maidservant
sections.gist: Where *bi'ah* as a mode of betrothal comes from; R. Abba bar Memel's objection that no betrothed virgin could otherwise exist; and what R. Yochanan learns from Rebbi's verse.

children.title: “Be'ulat Ba'al” or “U've'alah”? R. Yochanan and Rebbi's Verse
children.gist: R. Yochanan derives *bi'ah* from “*be'ulat ba'al*,” since Rebbi's verse alone might mean money followed by intercourse.

bullets.text: The Mishnah teaches that a woman is betrothed through intercourse. The source? R. Abbahu citing R. Yochanan: “a married woman (*be'ulat ba'al*)” (Devarim 22:22). He becomes her husband through intercourse.
R. Zeira to R. Abbahu (some say Reish Lakish to R. Yochanan): what is wrong with Rebbi's verse, “When a man takes a woman and engages in intercourse with her” (*u've'alah*, Devarim 24:1)?
Answer: from that verse alone one might say he must first betroth her with money and then have intercourse. “*Be'ulat ba'al*” teaches that intercourse alone betroths.

children.title: Where Is the Betrothed Virgin? R. Abba bar Memel's Objection
children.gist: If betrothal needed money plus intercourse, the stoning case of the *na'arah ha'me'orasah* could never arise. An answer from atypical intercourse fails on Abaye's rule; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak finds her in betrothal by document.

children.title: The Objection: Either Not a Virgin or Not Yet Betrothed
children.gist: On the money-plus-intercourse reading, a betrothed woman is either already a non-virgin or not yet betrothed.

bullets.text: R. Abba bar Memel: on that reading, how can there be a man stoned for intercourse with a betrothed young woman, the *na'arah ha'me'orasah* (Devarim 22:23–24)?
If he betrothed her with money and then had intercourse, she is a *be'ulah*, no longer a virgin, and stoning applies only for a virgin. If money without intercourse, the betrothal is not complete.

children.title: Atypical Intercourse by the Betrothed: Abaye and the Ten Men
children.gist: The Rabbis before Abaye suggest the betrothed completed the betrothal by atypical intercourse; Abaye answers that a husband's atypical intercourse makes her a non-virgin by all views.

bullets.text: The Rabbis before Abaye: she is found where the betrothed man had atypical (anal) intercourse with her, *shelo ke'darkah*. The betrothal is complete and she is still a virgin.
Abaye: Rebbi and the Rabbis disagree only about another man. For her husband, all agree that atypical intercourse makes her a *be'ulah*.

The dispute (Tosefta Sanhedrin 10:4): ten men had atypical intercourse with a betrothed young woman who is still a virgin. The Rabbis: all are stoned. Rebbi: the first is stoned and the rest strangled, since after the first she is no longer a virgin.
In law, the husband's marital act, vaginal or not, makes her a *be'ulah*, regardless of her physical state.

chart.caption: Atypical intercourse and virginity: the ten men (Tosefta Sanhedrin 10:4) and Abaye's rule
rows: Stoning: she is still a virgin
Strangulation: the first man made her a non-virgin

children.title: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Betrothal by Document
children.gist: A woman betrothed by document is fully betrothed with no further act, so she can be a betrothed virgin.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: she is found where he betrothed her by document.
All agree: since a document (a *get*) removes a woman from marriage completely with no further act, a document also brings her completely into betrothal. She is betrothed and still a virgin.

returns_to.note: Draws again on the parallel between the *get* and the betrothal document

children.title: “U've'alah” for R. Yochanan: A Wife, Not an *amah ivriyah*
children.gist: R. Yochanan uses Rebbi's verse to exclude an *amah ha'ivriyah* from acquisition by intercourse, blocking a *kal va'chomer* from the *yevamah* and a comparison to “another wife.”

bullets.text: What does R. Yochanan do with “and engages in intercourse with her”? It teaches that a wife is acquired through intercourse, but a Hebrew maidservant (*amah ha'ivriyah*) is not.

The verse is needed because one might argue *kal va'chomer* from a *yevamah*: she cannot be acquired with money, yet is acquired through intercourse; surely a maidservant, who can be acquired with money, is acquired through intercourse.
Refuted: a *yevamah* is different, since she is already bound to the *yavam* (*zekukah*).
Instead, one might argue from “If he take himself another wife” (Shemot 21:10), which sets the maidservant beside another wife, who is acquired through intercourse. The verse excludes this.

children.continues: Continues on 9b: Rebbi's source for excluding the maidservant (“with her” teaches two laws), Rava's use of the same verse for betrothal that can lead to consummation, and Rebbi's use of “*be'ulat ba'al*” for the husband's atypical intercourse.

key_terms.definition: One of the three modes of betrothal: the man gives the woman (or her father) a document stating that she is betrothed to him. It works through its words, not the value of the material.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks why the husband writes it, whose consent it needs for a minor and for a *bogeret*, and whether, like a *get*, it must be written for her and with her consent.

key_terms.sense: a document written for the specific woman
key_terms.definition: The requirement that a document such as a *get* be written for the sake of the particular woman and purpose it serves; one written generically (*shelo lishmah*) is invalid.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Reish Lakish rules that a betrothal document must be written *lishmah*, like a *get*, and the *amora'im* then dispute whether it also needs her knowledge.

key_terms.definition: The *hekesh* from “and she departs… and becomes” (Devarim 24:2) linking entering a marriage to leaving it, so that laws of divorce may be applied to betrothal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Reish Lakish uses it to require a betrothal document written for her; Rav Pappa shows how it yields both views on whether her consent is needed.

key_terms.sense: a woman past twelve and a half
key_terms.definition: A woman who has passed the stage of *na'arah*, about six months after puberty; she is no longer under her father's authority and betroths herself.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A betrothal document for a *bogeret* is addressed to her and needs her consent, unlike one for a minor, which is addressed to the father and needs his.

key_terms.definition: The third mode of betrothal, in which the man betroths the woman by intercourse performed for that purpose before witnesses.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yochanan derives it from “*be'ulat ba'al*,” since Rebbi's verse alone might suggest money followed by intercourse.

key_terms.definition: A young woman, betrothed but not yet married and still a virgin; a man who has intercourse with her willingly is liable to stoning rather than strangulation.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Abba bar Memel argues that if betrothal required money plus intercourse, this case could never arise; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak finds it in betrothal by document.

key_terms.definition: A woman who has had intercourse and so is legally no longer a virgin, with consequences for punishments, fines and the *ketubah*.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Abaye: a husband's atypical intercourse makes her a *be'ulah* by all views, whereas for another man Rebbi and the Rabbis disagree.

key_terms.definition: A Jewish girl sold by her father into service as a minor; the master or his son may later designate her as a wife.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yochanan learns from “and engages in intercourse with her” that she, unlike a wife, is not acquired through intercourse.

judgment_calls: The poor-person case (8b.14) is grouped with the double-language stories and the single-word dispute under one parent about replies that fail to accept; it could also stand alone as the tail of 8b's redirected-gift cases.
The three hilkheta rulings (9a.5) are a separate top-level section, not appended to the double-language section, because they settle disputes from earlier sugyot (silk, R. Elazar, collateral).
The minor/bogeret ruling (9a.11–12) is a sibling of 'Who Writes the Document' under the shtar section rather than a child of it, since it moves from direction of writing to whose consent counts.

The lishmah question, the consent dispute and the mishnah on documents of stipulation are grouped under 'Does the Shtar Follow the Get?' because all turn on how far the get governs the betrothal document; the stipulation-documents section could instead be a child of the consent dispute.
Line 9b.10 holds both the end of R. Abba bar Memel's objection and the Rabbis' answer before Abaye, so s20 and s21 both anchor to it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer (9b.13) stays inside the bi'ah section where the text places it, with a returns_to link to the get/shtar parallel.

R. Yochanan's use of 'u've'alah' (9b.14–16) is kept as the last child of the bi'ah section with a returns_to link, rather than a new top-level section, since it answers what R. Yochanan does with Rebbi's verse.
coverage_notes: The shiur's opening segment on Rav Mari's unresolved dog-distraction case (8b.12–13) falls before this outline's scope and is left out.
The essay describes the wares in the first story as buttons (citing Rashi as tin buttons); the text has strings of glass beads. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the hilkheta on partial payment to 'R. Eliezer'; the text has R. Elazar. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the minor/adult ruling to 'Rav Amram in the name of Rav Nachman'; the text has Rava in the name of Rav Nachman. Followed the text.
The essay names the challenger on the direction of writing as R. Zeira; the text (9a.7) has R. Zeira bar Memel. Followed the text.

The essay says the reading 'ki yukach' is 'rejected from' the verse 'I gave my daughter'; in the text that verse supports rereading 'ki yikach' as 'ki yakiach', which is why Rava abandons the verse-based answer. Followed the text.
The essay calls the source 'ein kotvim shtarei eirusin…' a braita; the text calls it a mishnah (Bava Batra 167b). Followed the text.
The essay omits the alternate attribution at 9b.7 ('some say it was Reish Lakish who said this to R. Yochanan'); included from the text.
The essay says the rejected reading needs 'money or shtar' plus intercourse; the text speaks of betrothal through money then intercourse. Followed the text.

The essay's statements that the silk ruling follows Rabba against Rav Yosef, and that under R. Elazar he owes the rest, are not in this daf's text; the first is kept as shiur material, the second omitted.
